verdict: Avoid new petrochemicals exposure in Haldia for now; the Adperma phenol/acetone start-up is a real structural positive, but West Bengal demand signals and national petrochemical output are both negative, so lend only to integrated, feedstock-linked downstream units with tight structure.
title: Haldia Petrochemicals: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Petrochemicals in Haldia is a conversion business: propylene and feedstock go in, phenol, acetone and downstream chemicals come out, and cash is made on the spread between feedstock cost and product price.** The anchor event is Adperma's new phenol and acetone plant at Haldia, with capacity of 345,000 metric tons of phenol and 215,000 mt of acetone, a 60 billion Indian rupees ($630 million) project [2]. It is feedstock-integrated with Haldia Petrochemicals' ecosystem and has road, rail, waterway and pipeline connectivity [2]. **Value sits in integration and logistics, not in the molecule itself** — the plant is positioned to cut India's reliance on imported phenol and acetone [2]. ## What has changed now
**The local demand picture is weak even as new capacity lands.** West Bengal GST collections are -1.3% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, 7.4 pp slower [D], and state electricity demand is +5.7% against India +9.5%, 3.8 pp slower [D]. Nationally, IIP NIC 20 output is -0.5% YoY and -1.2% Apr-to-date [D]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's offtake is export-linked or tied to the new Adperma chain; if it is purely eastern-India domestic downstream, ask who the end customer is and what volume commitment they have given.** Adperma targets production by December 2026 [1], so commissioning risk is live right now. ## Where the growth is
**Pursue borrowers that plug into the new phenolics chain: tanker-loading, storage, pipeline and utility service providers, and downstream converters who can show an Adperma or HPL supply or offtake link** [2]. The project inauguration was treated as a marker of renewed large industry investment in Haldia after roughly two decades [3]. **Avoid standalone traders and small converters with no feedstock linkage and no contracted offtake** — they carry price risk on both ends. Peer results are strong but not local: Reliance's oil-to-chemicals segment hit record operating profitability [5] and Gandhar Oil reported Q2 FY27 revenue of INR 1,847 crores, up ~73% YoY [6]; read these as evidence of the cycle, not of Haldia demand. ## How to grow safely
**Structure against the conversion cycle, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock and book-debt statements, feedstock purchase invoices and product sale invoices, and a monthly drawing-power or offtake confirmation from the anchor buyer. **If the borrower's receivable days stretch beyond the stated credit terms, ask for the ageing and the buyer-wise breakup before any enhancement.** Rating support is mixed: ICRA upgraded HPL's long-term rating to A- [11], while another ICRA note keeps a company on watch over a proposed amalgamation and capex clarity [8]. Note that the CRISIL petrochemical criteria documents are old and generic [9][10] — use them for framework only. ## Early-warning signs
**Watch inventory days and spread compression first.** If phenol or acetone realisations fall while feedstock cost holds, the converter's margin goes before its sales do. **If monthly GST filings show turnover falling below the sanctioned drawing power for two consecutive months, freeze enhancement and re-price.** If Adperma's December 2026 start-up slips [1], treat every borrower whose plan depends on that offtake as unproven. Sources say little specific about Haldia's own credit behaviour, so lean on these first principles and the peer read-across.
